segments.narration: A government threatened archaeologists for saying who built this. Rhodesia would allow any answer except the correct one.
Great Zimbabwe is a stone city in southern Africa, raised from the eleventh century by ancestors of the Shona.
The Great Enclosure runs 250 metres around and rises eleven metres. Granite blocks, fitted dry. There is no mortar holding any of it.
In 1871 Karl Mauch decided Africans could not have built it and sold Europe a story about the Queen of Sheba. It stuck for decades.
Randall-MacIver disproved it in 1905. Caton-Thompson confirmed it in 1929. Rhodesia kept leaning on archaeologists anyway, and some left the country.

verdicts.claim: Rhodesian authorities pressured archaeologists not to say publicly that Great Zimbabwe was built by Africans.
verdicts.note: 75% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.note: 77% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: The Great Enclosure's outer wall runs about 250 metres with a maximum height of 11 metres, built dry-stone without mortar.
verdicts.note: 69% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Karl Mauch in 1871 discounted native construction and promoted a legend linking the site to the Queen of Sheba.
verdicts.note: Mauch (1871) discounted native construction and promoted the Queen of Sheba legend, claiming a lintel was Lebanese cedar brought by Phoenicians.

verdicts.claim: David Randall-MacIver concluded in 1905 that the structures were African, and Gertrude Caton-Thompson confirmed Bantu origin in 1929.
verdicts.note: Randall-MacIver concluded in 1905 the ruins were medieval and of exclusively African origin; Caton-Thompson confirmed Bantu origin in 1929.
